headline_en: Why Bangladesh is falling behind in sending skilled nurses abroad
summary_en: An opinion column by three researchers at the Centre for Migration Studies, North South University, builds on a 16 February 2025 speech by Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus, who said Bangladesh cannot produce skilled nurses for foreign demand and that many Bangladeshi workers go abroad with fake certificates. The authors cite global nurse demand figures, blame restricted BSc/MSc nursing education and gatekeeping by the Bangladesh Nursing and Midwifery Council, and argue that the lack of recognised skill certification and apprenticeship pushes workers toward fake certificates.

facts.statement: At the annual conference of the Bangladesh Administrative Service Association in Dhaka on 16 February 2025, Chief Adviser Prof. Muhammad Yunus said two problems are neglected: there is large demand for nurses abroad but Bangladesh cannot produce skilled nurses, and many Bangladeshi workers are going abroad to work with fake certificates.
facts.source_in_article: Muhammad Yunus, as cited by the column authors

facts.statement: A 2024 World Health Organization report is cited as saying about 29 crore nurses and 2.2 crore midwives currently work worldwide (figures as printed in the column), and that by 2030 there could be a shortage of about 4.5 crore nurses and 31 lakh midwives (as printed), hitting low and lower-middle income countries hardest.
facts.source_in_article: WHO 2024 report, as cited by the column authors

facts.statement: Registered nurses working: United States 3,175,390 in 2023; United Kingdom 748,000 in 2022; Germany 1,004,000 in 2022; Japan 1,734,000 in 2022; Saudi Arabia 235,461 in 2023.
facts.source_in_article: Government health agencies and statistics bureaus of the countries concerned, as cited by the column authors

facts.statement: About 640,000 nurses from India currently work abroad, mostly in the Middle East, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada and Australia; the demand is estimated to roughly double in the next six to seven years.
facts.source_in_article: Column authors (sources given: Reuters and Economic Times)

facts.statement: About 240,000 Filipino nurses were working abroad as of 2020, and 13,223 Filipino nursing professionals were newly deployed internationally in 2023; nurses' remittances to the Philippines are about USD 8 billion a year, about a quarter of that country's total remittances and about one tenth of GDP.
facts.source_in_article: Reuters and Economic Times, as cited by the column authors

facts.statement: Muhammad Yunus said developed countries including the United Kingdom and Japan have expressed interest in recruiting nurses from Bangladesh, and that Grameen Caledonian College of Nursing shows Bangladesh can train nurses of international standard who are able to work in various countries.
facts.source_in_article: Muhammad Yunus, as cited by the column authors

facts.statement: Many Bangladeshi nurses with practical experience and skill cannot get jobs abroad because they lack a recognised BSc or MSc degree; where the degree is available the curriculum is often weak or outdated and does not match international guidelines or competency standards.
facts.source_in_article: Column authors (Centre for Migration Studies, North South University)

facts.statement: BSc and MSc in Nursing programmes run only at Dhaka University, Bangladesh Medical University (formerly BSMMU), Chittagong, Rajshahi, Mymensingh and Khulna universities and Sylhet M A Gafur Medical University (as printed), with very limited seats, so thousands of students miss out each year.

The column says the Bangladesh Nursing and Midwifery Council (BNMC) acts as a gatekeeper by not permitting private universities to run nursing programmes, keeping the sector under government control, even though private medical colleges run MBBS programmes under public universities.

Grameen Caledonian College of Nursing operates with Health Ministry approval in partnership with an international university, but its students still have to receive their degree through Dhaka University so that the certificate is accepted internationally.

The column argues that agreements Bangladesh signs with labour-receiving countries often lack clear terms on recognition of work and skill certification, and that Bangladeshi workers have almost no access to apprenticeship or on-the-job-training certificates; a worker with some experience is treated as 'unskilled' when applying for another job, which pushes workers to present fake certificates.

The authors recommend that the government build an internationally accepted skill certification and apprenticeship system so that work experience gets formal recognition, with certificates that can be verified digitally to reduce forgery, and allow private-sector nursing education.

headline_en: Bhairab youth allegedly dies in Libya from torture by broker ring
summary_en: Sohag Mia (28) of Bhairab, Kishoreganj, died in Libya in the custody of a broker ring about seven months after being taken there under a BDT 16 lakh deal to reach Italy by sea. His family says the ring extracted the whole sum in instalments and tortured and starved him; the accused broker Sentu Mia is reportedly out of the country.

facts.statement: A broker ring agreed to take Sohag Mia (28) of Bhairab, Kishoreganj, to Italy by sea via Libya for BDT 16 lakh; he was taken to Libya about seven months before April 2025 after BDT 5 lakh was paid, and never reached Italy.

Sohag Mia's family paid the full BDT 16 lakh in instalments to brokers; BDT 5 lakh was paid before he was taken to Libya and the rest was extracted on various pretexts while he was held there. His elder brother Sujon Mia, who lives in Italy, says the brokers took the BDT 16 lakh through him.

Sohag Mia (28) of Kalipur Dakshinpara, Bhairab municipality, Kishoreganj, died in Libya in the custody of a broker ring; the family alleges continuous physical and mental torture, inadequate food, and that he fell ill after a beating a few days earlier and was not taken to hospital.

The ring held Sohag Mia in Libya and collected the whole contract money in instalments on pretexts without sending him on; when he raised the matter he was physically and mentally tortured, and his wife Liza Begum says she could only talk to him after paying money the brokers demanded.

Sohag Mia met a broker named Sentu Mia of Baroicha area, Belabo upazila, Narsingdi, while in Bangladesh, and contracted through him to go to Italy by sea via Libya; sources say Sentu Mia is currently not in Bangladesh and his mobile phone is switched off. After the death none of the brokers could be reached by phone.
facts.source_in_article: Family members; unnamed sources cited by reporter

facts.statement: The family asked for government help to bring Sohag Mia's body home from Libya and demanded trial of the broker ring; Bhairab Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Shabnam Sharmin said she would cooperate in bringing the body back.
Sohag Mia had earlier worked in Qatar for 8 years and returned to Bangladesh about a year before, married, and has a two-month-old daughter.

headline_en: Amin-Swapan ring plotting a syndicate again for Malaysia, say BAIRA leaders
summary_en: On 5 February 2025 a group of BAIRA (recruiting agency owners' association) leaders gave a memorandum to the expatriates' welfare ministry secretary alleging that the syndicate of Malaysian national Amin Noor and his Bangladeshi partner Ruhul Amin alias Swapan extorted BDT 1,07,000 per worker sent to Malaysia and is trying to form a syndicate again. The memorandum also asks for Saudi visas in lots of up to 24 to get emigration clearance without embassy attestation and for action against air-ticket hoarding.

facts.statement: BAIRA leaders allege that the syndicate of Malaysian national Amin Noor and his Bangladeshi partner Ruhul Amin alias Swapan extorted BDT 1 lakh 7 thousand per worker for sending workers to Malaysia, and demand strict legal action against the two as the syndicate's ringleaders.
facts.source_in_article: Memorandum by BAIRA leaders to the Secretary, Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment

facts.statement: A section of BAIRA held a human chain in front of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment saying the Amin-Swapan ring is manoeuvring to form a syndicate again around the reopening of the Malaysian labour market, and demanded steps so no syndicate is formed again.
The memorandum was signed by 12 BAIRA members including Riazul Islam, Noman Chowdhury, Khandaker Abu Ashfaq and Md. Fakhrul Islam, some of them top leaders of BAIRA's recently dissolved committee.

For Saudi Arabia, the current rule is that more than one visa (a visa lot of more than one) must be attested by the embassy before emigration clearance; earlier up to 25 visas were exempt. BAIRA leaders demand that up to 24 visas be treated as a single item and given emigration clearance without embassy attestation.

The memorandum says a syndicate hoards air tickets every year and sells them at double the price or more, leaving poor outbound workers ruined; BAIRA leaders demand action and the introduction of a 'labour fare' for migrant workers.

headline_en: Witness believes from the bodies' appearance that all are Bangladeshi
summary_en: A boat carrying 56 people from Libya toward Italy sank in the Mediterranean on 25 January 2025; 23 decomposed bodies washed ashore in eastern Libya between 28 and 31 January and were buried in the Ajdabiya area. The Bangladesh embassy in Tripoli, citing local sources, the Red Crescent and a Bangladeshi who helped wash the bodies, says nearly all appear to be Bangladeshi; two survivors are in hospital and the rest are missing.

facts.statement: A boat with 56 people aboard left the Libyan coast for Italy on the night of 25 January 2025 and sank in the Mediterranean, most likely the same night.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Ambassador to Libya Maj. Gen. Abul Hasnat Mohammad Khairul Bashar, video message on embassy Facebook page

facts.statement: 23 bodies washed up on Libya's eastern coast: 7 on 28 January, 11 on 29 January, 3 on 30 January and 2 on 31 January 2025; they were decomposed, carried no documents, and were buried in the Ajdabiya (printed 'Ajdadia') area.

The identity of the 23 bodies was not confirmed, but the Bangladesh embassy in Libya, citing local sources, says nearly all were Bangladeshi; the Libyan Red Cross/Red Crescent, based on those involved in recovery and burial, said all 23 were Bangladeshi. A Bangladeshi who helped wash the bodies at Ajdabiya hospital in the Brega region thought from their appearance that all were Bangladeshi.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy in Tripoli report to the Foreign Ministry

facts.statement: Two people rescued in critical condition were under close observation in a hospital (described as controlled by Benghazi militia, or an army or police hospital) and their identity was not confirmed; the fate of the remaining 31 was unknown.

The Bangladesh embassy had asked the authorities for permission to travel to the Brega area but had not received it. Eastern Libya's Benghazi is controlled by General Haftar's forces, with whom Bangladesh has not managed to establish direct contact; the embassy is using an organisation named Dar-Al Libya (printed 'দ্বার-আল লিবিয়া'), the local Red Crescent Society and relatives to get information on the living and dead.

headline_en: Sumon of Bhairab never reached Italy; dies in Libya allegedly from broker torture
summary_en: Sumon Mia (42), a rice trader from Bhairab, Kishoreganj, left Bangladesh four months earlier to reach Italy, paid brokers BDT 18 lakh in instalments, and died in Libya; his family learned of the death on about 29 January 2025 and alleges torture by the broker ring. Broker Sweety Begum, who took BDT 10 lakh, denies torture and says the death was natural.

facts.statement: Sumon Mia (42) of Lakshmipur area, Bhairab municipality, Kishoreganj, paid a broker ring a total of BDT 18 lakh in several instalments to reach Italy; BDT 10 lakh of it was taken by Sweety Begum on a promise to deliver him to Italy by sea, and the rest went to another broker. The money was raised by selling land and gold jewellery and borrowing.

Sumon Mia reached Libya on his own initiative about four months before February 2025; there he met a broker called 'Dada', through whom he was introduced to Sweety Begum of Shambhupur village, Shibpur union, Bhairab, whose husband Mozammel Haque sends people to Italy. The promise was to deliver him to Italy by sea on 24 January 2025.

The family of Sumon Mia (42) received news on Wednesday, about 29 January 2025, that he had died in Libya without reaching Italy; the family alleges the death was not natural and was caused by torture by the broker ring. He last spoke to his wife on 23 January, saying the brokers were stalling.
After the death news, broker Sweety told Sumon's wife that he had reached Italy and did not admit the death; the Libya-based broker did not answer phone calls.

Sweety Begum, who is currently in Bangladesh, said she had made all arrangements to get Sumon to Italy and could do nothing if someone dies before reaching the destination; she claimed the death was natural and that no physical or mental torture took place.

Bhairab UNO Shabnam Sharmin said Sumon had tried to go to Italy illegally, that the administration was checking whether the ministry knew of the death and, if not, would inform it in writing and apply to get the body back.

headline_en: Expatriates bent under the weight of duty: a human form of the honeybee's life
summary_en: A reader's essay by Rahman Mridha in the diaspora section compares the lives of Bangladesh's more than one crore expatriates to honeybees who never taste their honey. It lists general obstacles (broker fraud, administrative corruption, weak legal protection, lack of social recognition) and proposals (free skill and language training, going only through approved agencies, hotline, compulsory insurance, a central online platform, investment incentives). It contains no specific cases, figures or procedures.

facts.statement: The essay puts the number of Bangladeshi expatriates at more than one crore.

The essay says many migrants fall into broker rings that take everything on false promises of visa and work and abandon them midway, and that returnees face bribes when seeking government help and poor protection in land and savings disputes; it proposes free vocational and language training centres, internationally recognised skill certificates, migration only through approved recruiting agencies, a special law against broker rings, an international hotline, compulsory health and travel insurance for outgoing workers, a central online platform for expatriates' applications, and tax and banking incentives for investment.
facts.source_in_article: Essay author Rahman Mridha (a self-described long-time expatriate)

headline_en: Call for multiple-entry visas for Bangladeshi workers
summary_en: Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus, meeting Malaysian High Commissioner Mohd Shuhada Othman at the State Guest House Jamuna, asked Malaysia to give Bangladeshi workers multiple-entry visas and to let in the 18,000 workers who missed the May 2024 deadline. The High Commissioner said a joint technical committee had been formed, met in Kuala Lumpur on 31 December and was to meet again. The rest of the article covers an unrelated university election.

facts.statement: Chief Adviser Prof. Muhammad Yunus called on Malaysia to give Bangladeshi workers multiple-entry visas (one visa allowing several trips), saying this would let workers return home easily when needed; he made the call when Malaysian High Commissioner in Dhaka Mohd Shuhada Othman (মোহাম্মদ সুহাদা ওসমান) met him at the State Guest House Jamuna on a Monday (article published 13 January 2025).
Yunus also called on Malaysia to ensure entry for the 18,000 Bangladeshi workers who could not join work in Malaysia within the deadline set in May 2024.

The Malaysian High Commissioner said a joint technical committee of Malaysian and Bangladeshi officials had been formed on the matter of the 18,000 workers; it met in Kuala Lumpur on 31 December 2024 and was due to meet again on the Tuesday after the Jamuna meeting (about 14 January 2025).
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian High Commissioner Mohd Shuhada Othman

facts.statement: Yunus expressed hope that Malaysia would move the process quickly so the next group of Bangladeshi workers can plan to go to Malaysia, and referred to his October 2024 meeting in Dhaka with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

headline_en: 48% of returned migrants' health problems are mental
summary_en: A study by the grassroots migrant organisation OKUP (Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program), presented in Dhaka on 29 December 2024, found that of 1,830 returned migrant workers who sought services, 1,096 (60%) came for health care and 48% of those for mental health problems; the survey covered returnees from six Middle East countries in seven districts. It also reports migration costs paid by women and men and two returnee women's accounts of abuse and deception in Saudi Arabia.

facts.statement: OKUP found that 1,830 returned migrant workers took various services; 60% or 1,096 came for health care, and 48% of those came with mental health problems. Of those who came, 61% were women and 39% men, but 53% of those with mental health problems were men.
facts.source_in_article: OKUP (Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program) survey report presented 29 December 2024

facts.statement: The OKUP survey covered 1,096 returnees from 6 Middle East countries who came back between 2020 and 2023; data were collected from March to June 2024 in Cumilla, Dhaka, Faridpur, Narsingdi, Narayanganj, Manikganj and Munshiganj districts, with in-depth interviews and group discussions. The report is titled (in Bangla) 'Health of Bangladeshi migrant workers: the burden of hidden migration cost on socio-economic development'. 55% of respondents had returned from Saudi Arabia.
The OKUP report says women have no (official) migration cost, yet 21% of 666 women said they had to spend BDT 2 to 3 lakh; 29% of male workers said they had to spend more than BDT 6 lakh.

Health problems returnees came back with include back pain, workplace accident injuries, heart disease, kidney problems, cancer, high blood pressure, tumours and skin disease; mental health complaints were highest among domestic workers, followed by agriculture, construction and cleaning workers. Some migrants borrowed money from home for treatment, and many returned because they could not get treatment abroad.

Shefali Begum of Narsingdi, who went to Saudi Arabia lured by a broker, said she was made to do a lot of work without being given food, the male householder physically abused her and beat her when she complained, broke her hand and gave no treatment; she then returned to Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Shefali Begum, at the OKUP event

facts.statement: Returnee Shefali Begum of Narsingdi filed a case against the broker but, under pressure from local people, settled with the broker for BDT 30,000 compensation and withdrew the case.
facts.source_in_article: Shefali Begum, at the OKUP event

facts.statement: Mosammat Hanifa of Narayanganj paid a broker BDT 4 lakh to go to Saudi Arabia for a company job; on arrival there was no job, she was kept in a room with 20 to 25 people for some days, made to work one month in pilgrims' (hajis') houses and then turned out; she then worked illegally in various places, fell ill, and returned with kidney problems and diabetes and is still under treatment.
facts.source_in_article: Mosammat Hanifa, at the OKUP event

facts.statement: Joint Secretary Mohammad Shahin of the expatriates' welfare ministry said ensuring regular migration would solve more than 50% of the problems, that there is a coordination gap, and that a way must be found for migrants to lodge complaints instantly. BMET deputy director Rezwanul Haque Chowdhury said the ministry has the smallest budget and staff. Wage Earners' Welfare Board deputy director Shariful Islam said workers must also take responsibility and that proper training and awareness reduce problems.
facts.source_in_article: Officials speaking at the OKUP event

facts.statement: Sumaiya Islam, executive director of Bangladesh Nari Sramik Kendra, said remittances have not risen in line with the numbers who went to the Middle East, meaning not everyone found work, that women workers there cannot leave the house, and that the Welfare Board's money should be used to support migrant workers instead of lying idle. OKUP chairperson Shakirul Islam said men's mental health is neglected while services exist for women.

headline_en: Migration to Malaysia's plantation sector
summary_en: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment issued a notice on hiring Bangladeshi workers for Malaysia's plantation sector, with 31 January 2025 as the last date of entry. It sets the government migration fee at BDT 78,990, lists steps to finish by 15 January 2025 and tells workers to verify agents via the ministry website or call centre 16135.

facts.statement: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment issued a notice on recruitment of Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia's plantation sector; the last date for Bangladeshi workers to enter Malaysia for this sector is 31 January 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment notice

facts.statement: Workers going to Malaysia's plantation sector must complete the medical test, obtain the visa, get BMET (Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training) clearance, attend pre-departure orientation and confirm the air ticket by 15 January 2025.
The government-fixed migration fee for Malaysia's plantation sector is BDT 78,990; no money beyond this is to be paid to a recruiting agent or anyone else.

The ministry tells Malaysia-bound plantation workers to learn the job terms, pay and benefits fully from the recruiting agent, to have no money dealings with anyone other than an approved recruiting agent, and to make every payment against a proper written receipt/document or through a bank account.

Workers should verify which recruiting agents and organisations are permitted for the Malaysia plantation recruitment on the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment website or by calling its call centre 16135.
The ministry said that if the Malaysian government issues any instruction on this matter, everyone concerned will be informed.

headline_en: 150 Bangladeshis return from Libya
summary_en: More than 150 Bangladeshis stranded in Libya returned to Dhaka on a chartered flight on 10 October 2024, in a repatriation by the Foreign Ministry, the Bangladesh embassy in Tripoli and IOM. Most had entered Libya illegally through traffickers hoping to reach Europe by sea, and many had been kidnapped and tortured; IOM gave each BDT 6,000 and other support.

facts.statement: More than 150 Bangladeshis stranded in Libya arrived in Dhaka on a chartered flight on the morning of Thursday 10 October 2024; the repatriation was a joint effort of the Foreign Ministry, the Bangladesh embassy in Tripoli and the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
Most of the returnees had entered Libya illegally, influenced by human traffickers, with the aim of reaching Europe by sea; many were kidnapped and tortured in Libya.

IOM gave each returnee from Libya a grant of BDT 6,000, food and medical assistance and, where needed, temporary accommodation; Foreign Ministry and IOM officials received them at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.
Foreign Ministry officials urged the returnees to raise awareness about irregular migration, especially the dangerous journey to Europe via Libya.

headline_en: Interest in going abroad on bank loans is rising
summary_en: A feature on Probashi Kallyan Bank (PKB), the state bank for migrants: it lends up to BDT 3 lakh without collateral to people going abroad for work, at 9% simple interest, and also lends to returnees. The article gives loan terms, eligibility and documents, loan types, deposit schemes, the loan-risk cover scheme, branch numbers and lending statistics up to FY2023-24.

facts.statement: Probashi Kallyan Bank (PKB) lends up to BDT 3 lakh to unemployed men and women going abroad for work, repayable in monthly instalments, with no movable or immovable property required as collateral; it also has loans for self-employment of people who have returned from abroad.

PKB migration loan terms: maximum BDT 3 lakh, set according to visa validity; loan term 3 years for a new visa and 2 years for a re-entry visa; 2-month grace period before repayment; interest 9% simple interest.

If all documents are in order, PKB communicates its loan decision within seven days of application; after the application process the bank informs the applicant of loan approval by SMS to the mobile phone.
Applying for a PKB loan costs nothing; the application is made on the bank's prescribed form, and the customer must open an account with the bank before taking the loan.
A valid visa is a main condition for a PKB migration loan, together with the appointment letter issued by the company that will employ the worker abroad.

Applicant's documents for a PKB migration loan: four attested passport-size photos, a certificate from the municipality or union parishad showing present and permanent address, copies of passport and visa, photocopy of the manpower smart card, and photocopy of the national ID (NID).

A PKB migration loan needs two guarantors, each giving one passport-size photo, NID and a municipality or union parishad certificate of present and permanent address, plus three bank cheque leaves signed by any one of the guarantors.

PKB has six loan types: migration loan, rehabilitation loan, special rehabilitation loan, Bangabandhu migrant large family loan, self-employment loan, and women's migration and rehabilitation loan. Loan instalments can be paid at any Sonali Bank branch as well as PKB branches, under an agreement between the two banks.

Every PKB migration-loan borrower must pay a subscription and join the 'loan risk cover scheme' (ঋণ ঝুঁকি আচ্ছাদন স্কিম): if the borrower dies during the loan term, 100% of the outstanding balance is waived; if the borrower returns from abroad within six months of taking the loan, 50% of the outstanding balance is waived.
PKB has waived BDT 2 crore 74 lakh of loans of 168 borrowers who died at home or abroad after taking a loan.

PKB managing director Mojibur Rahman said the bank waives even the principal if a customer dies abroad, lends to returnee women for self-employment at 4 to 7% interest, and has kept the migration loan rate at 9% despite rising bank interest rates.
facts.source_in_article: Mojibur Rahman, Managing Director, Probashi Kallyan Bank

facts.statement: PKB deposit schemes for migrant workers and their families: Bangabandhu savings scheme, Bangabandhu education savings scheme, marriage savings scheme, Bangabandhu double benefit savings scheme and PKB school banking savings scheme; public response is low because deposit interest is low.
PKB has 122 branches nationwide (65 at district level and 57 at upazila level), plus one arrival booth and one departure booth at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.
From its founding in 2011 to FY2023-24, PKB lent BDT 3,311 crore 86 lakh to 170,194 migrants; in its first year, FY2011-12, it lent BDT 7 crore 34 lakh to 899 people.

PKB loans are most applied for by people going to Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Oman, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain; applications for Italy, Romania, South Korea and Singapore are also rising.

PKB was inaugurated on 20 April 2011 and listed by Bangladesh Bank as a scheduled specialised bank on 30 July 2018; authorised and paid-up capital is BDT 500 crore, 95% from the Wage Earners' Welfare Board and 5% from the government, and a proposal to raise paid-up capital to BDT 2,000 crore is with the Finance Division. Its four aims: help unemployed people go abroad for work, help them find work on return, help expatriates invest at home, and help send remittances quickly and cheaply.
PKB's default loan rate was 12% two years earlier and has fallen to 7.4% after 15 regional offices were set up.
facts.source_in_article: Mojibur Rahman, Managing Director, Probashi Kallyan Bank

headline_en: Joint task force of the two countries will work to protect Saudi-bound workers from fraud: foreign minister
summary_en: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud told expatriates at the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh on 1 July 2024 that a Bangladesh-Saudi joint task force will work to protect Bangladeshis seeking jobs in Saudi Arabia from fraud. He listed government measures for expatriates and promised to address their demands, and adviser Salman F Rahman urged would-be migrants to verify the employer before going.

facts.statement: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud said a Bangladesh-Saudi Arabia joint task force will work to protect Bangladeshis who want to go to Saudi Arabia for jobs from being cheated; he said he had fruitful talks with the Saudi foreign minister on forming the task force to bring more transparency to manpower export and stop harassment of workers by vested interests.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud, speaking at the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh (press release)

facts.statement: Hasan Mahmud listed government measures for expatriates: incentive on sending remittances, foreign-currency accounts through online offshore banking, the universal pension scheme, and loans through Probashi Kallyan Bank.

The foreign minister assured expatriates in Saudi Arabia that their demands would be addressed: more skilled Bangladeshi professionals hired, easier iqama renewal, a direct Chattogram-Riyadh flight, Wage Earners' Bond, health insurance for expatriates, better arrangements to bring home bodies of deceased expatriates, legal aid, passport renewal through the embassy, correction of NID information, and renewal of family visas.

Salman F Rahman, the Prime Minister's adviser on private industry and investment, said Bangladeshis interested in going to Saudi Arabia need to verify the genuineness of the employer before going, and asked expatriates living in Saudi Arabia to raise awareness so newcomers are not cheated. The foreign minister told expatriates to obey local laws.

headline_en: Corruption, broker rings and quotas: where can the unemployed go
summary_en: A column by Prothom Alo joint editor Sohrab Hassan on the June 2024 budget, unemployment and the civil-service quota ruling. Its migration content is two examples: Seema Akter of Sirajganj, taken to India irregularly by a broker in March 2022 and jailed for two years, and the roughly 17,000 Malaysia-bound workers who could not fly despite visas and work permits after each paying over BDT 5 lakh.

facts.statement: Seema Akter of Sirajganj Sadar upazila went to India irregularly through a broker in March 2022 on the promise of beauty-parlour work; she was detained by law enforcers on the way to Bengaluru, served a two-year sentence for illegal entry, and returned to her family after about two and a half years through the Bangladesh Assistant High Commission in Agartala.
facts.source_in_article: Columnist Sohrab Hassan, citing a Prothom Alo online report published on budget day (6 June 2024)

facts.statement: After Malaysia decided 'last year' (the column is dated June 2024) to take several lakh workers from Bangladesh following a third closure, 17,000 workers could not go despite getting visas and work permits; the column says each of them had paid more than BDT 5 lakh to so-called agencies.

Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics counts 25 lakh 90 thousand unemployed (average 24 lakh 70 thousand at end of 2023), a figure the columnist calls unbelievable; BIDS research found 66% of National University master's degree holders unemployed.

headline_en: Recruiters put the blame on the Malaysian government for workers failing to go
summary_en: At a 4 June 2024 press briefing by the panel of 101 agencies approved for Malaysia, BAIRA leaders and MP-recruiters blamed the two governments for the agency-selection 'syndicate' and blamed Malaysia for workers being unable to travel before the deadline. They said 16,970 workers with BMET clearance could not go, that Malaysia blacklisted 47 companies near the end, and that migration costs would be refunded through the main agency if diplomatic efforts fail.

facts.statement: 16,970 workers could not go to Malaysia despite having BMET clearance.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter; discussed at the 101-agency panel press briefing

facts.statement: Near the end of the recruitment window Malaysia blacklisted 47 companies on various complaints, and workers whose visas were issued in those companies' names could not go; the briefing said few missed out because of air tickets and that on average 2 to 3 percent of cleared workers drop out for various reasons.

BAIRA secretary general Ali Haider Chowdhury said the last-minute pressure would not have arisen if Malaysia had stopped issuing visas from 15 May; Ruhul Amin said Malaysia kept issuing visas to the end, with some receiving theirs on 30 May, so the number needing special flights could not be estimated and those people could not be sent.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Haider Chowdhury; Ruhul Amin alias Swapan

facts.statement: Ruhul Amin alias Swapan said the real number of workers who could not go is 5,000 to 6,000; the government is making diplomatic efforts to send them and, if that fails, their migration cost will be returned: affected people who apply will get the money back from the main agency.
facts.source_in_article: Ruhul Amin alias Swapan, former BAIRA secretary general

facts.statement: Ali Haider Chowdhury said the number of affected workers is not confirmed; a ministry-formed investigation committee will prepare the list of affected people and BAIRA will assist it.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Haider Chowdhury, BAIRA secretary general

facts.statement: 101 agencies got the chance to send workers to Malaysia; BAIRA leaders say Malaysia finalised the agency list and the Bangladesh government agreed to give Malaysia that choice in the agreement. The 101 include the state agency BOESL, Md. Noor Ali's Unique Eastern Private Limited (printed 'ইউনিট ইস্টার্ন প্রাইভেট লিমিটেড') and agencies owned by MPs; earlier Malaysia had selected 10 agencies.
facts.source_in_article: BAIRA president Mohammad Abul Bashar; secretary general Ali Haider Chowdhury; written statement; MP Benjir Ahmed

facts.statement: MP Nizam Uddin Hazari said 'there is no such word as syndicate', that the Malaysian government selected the agencies and 'coincidentally we were also selected', and that he was not involved in sending workers or buying and selling visas and only did processing. MP and former BAIRA president Benjir Ahmed said he did not lobby and that legal action will be taken against anyone involved in corruption. MP Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury attended but did not speak.

The panel's written statement accused a group led by Noor Ali of running media propaganda for business gain and BAIRA election advantage, although he does business with Malaysia in his own and other names.

summary_en: On 20 March 2024 the Bangladesh Civil Society for Migrants (BCSM), a platform of 23 organisations, said more than 4 lakh Bangladeshis have gone to Malaysia since 2022 through the recruiting agencies' syndicate system, and that excessive migration cost and months without work have become widespread. headline_en: Why Rohingyas are desperate to migrate by illegal routes
summary_en: A column by researchers at North South University's Centre for Migration Studies, based on ongoing interviews in Teknaf and Ukhia, explains why Rohingya refugees (and local Bangladeshis) attempt the irregular sea route from Teknaf to Malaysia. It describes the route via the Myanmar coast, the cost of BDT 4 to 5 lakh, UNHCR figures on attempts and deaths, and the push factors in the camps, including marriage offers used to move young girls.

facts.statement: Traffickers first take Malaysia-bound Bangladeshis and Rohingya refugees to Teknaf, Cox's Bazar; from Teknaf they go by boat to the Myanmar-Bangladesh sea border and then by small boat to the 'Samila' (সামিলা) coast of Myanmar, crammed in large numbers into small boats; the groups always include many women, children and newborns.
facts.source_in_article: Centre for Migration Studies (North South University) researchers, from interviews

facts.statement: Migrants pay traffickers in advance at Samila for the onward journey to Malaysia or Australia, and in some cases more is extracted than was promised in Teknaf; returned migrants say going to Malaysia this way costs BDT 4 to 5 lakh.
facts.source_in_article: Returned migrants interviewed by Centre for Migration Studies

facts.statement: According to UNHCR, 8,312 Rohingya refugees tried to reach Malaysia by sea in 2018-22; 589 of them drowned and many went missing.
facts.source_in_article: UNHCR, as cited by the column authors

facts.statement: UNHCR and Bangladesh government data show about 970,000 Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh as of November 2023, of whom only 31,439 were moved to Bhasan Char.
facts.source_in_article: UNHCR and Government of Bangladesh, as cited by the column authors

facts.statement: Traffickers use relatives and friends of Rohingya already in Malaysia, and social media (Facebook, imo, WhatsApp), to persuade camp residents to go; Rohingya men in Malaysia offer dowry-free marriage to the guardians of young girls and say the wife can then travel safely to Malaysia.

Of those who take the sea route, some die at sea, some who survive are sold as slaves in Myanmar, and some who reach Malaysia are sold there and cut off from contact with their families; many fail and come back.

The column says Rohingya earlier blended into local Bangladeshi society and went to Middle East and South-East Asian countries on Bangladeshi passports, and warns that if Rohingya travel to Malaysia on Bangladeshi passports does not fall, Bangladesh will become known as a human-trafficking country. Bangladesh was Tier 2 in the US State Department's 2022 Trafficking in Persons report.

Push factors reported from the camps: families of six to eight in a small space with usually one earner, no recognised way to work locally, the World Food Programme allocation cut from BDT 1,200 to BDT 800, and frequent kidnappings and killings by criminal groups in the camps. Rohingya also try irregular routes to Indonesia, Thailand and Australia.
facts.source_in_article: Rohingya interviewees and camp leaders (majhis), via Centre for Migration Studies

headline_en: Employment agreement with Japan; worker recruitment to start from 1 April
summary_en: Bangladesh and Japan signed the 'Memorandum of Cooperation on Employment Skills Development' (ESDP-MoC) on 17 October 2026; Japan will start recruiting Bangladeshi workers under it from 1 April of the following year. The agreement runs five years with automatic five-year extension and promises legal protection equal to Japanese workers, including no dismissal for pregnancy or childbirth.

facts.statement: Bangladesh and Japan signed the 'Memorandum of Cooperation on Employment Skills Development' (ESDP-MoC) on 17 October 2026; Japan will begin recruiting Bangladeshi workers under it from 1 April of the next year (article published 19 October 2026).
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: The ESDP-MoC has an initial term of five years and renews automatically for another five, for a total of 10 years. It was signed by the Secretary of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment for Bangladesh and by representatives of Japan's Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare and National Police Agency.

Under the ESDP-MoC, Bangladeshi workers will get legal protection equal to Japan's local workers and equal opportunity for men and women at work; women foreign workers cannot be dismissed or discriminated against because of pregnancy or childbirth, and the agreement contains no mandatory provision for forced return home on that ground.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury

facts.statement: The minister said the agreement will create opportunities for skills development, higher pay and long-term residence in Japan for Bangladeshi workers; copies of the agreement will be formally exchanged during Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's upcoming Japan visit.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury; ministry press release

headline_en: Failure to protect expatriates is not acceptable in any way
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial on the execution of two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia for 'immoral acts', which the Jeddah consulate learned of only after the Saudi interior ministry statement appeared on the Saudi Press Agency. It criticises the mission's failure to know of the trial, cites Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations and OKUP research on abuse of women workers, and lists four steps the government should take.

facts.statement: Two Bangladeshis were executed in Saudi Arabia for 'immoral acts' (অনৈতিক কাজ); the Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah learned of it only after the Saudi interior ministry's statement was published by the Saudi Press Agency, although the trial ran for months, the verdict was upheld by a higher authority and carried out by royal order.

Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, to which both Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia are parties, sets out the right to consular contact for an accused national; the editorial says arranging consular contact, a lawyer and an interpreter and monitoring the trial fall within a mission's duties, and that it is not known whether the accused asked for the consulate to be told.

About five days after the executions became public, Dhaka asked the Saudi ambassador to Bangladesh about the two Bangladeshis. The editorial criticises State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam for only advising citizens to take a 'lesson', and a ruling-party lawmaker's remark about not bringing home 'bodies of sin'.
OKUP (Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program) research found that 94% of women workers who were forced to return had suffered regular physical and mental abuse abroad and 47% had been sexually harassed.
facts.source_in_article: OKUP research, cited from Prothom Alo of 13 September 2026

facts.statement: The editorial states that several countries have been able to avert executions of their nationals in Saudi Arabia through strong diplomatic contact, and that bodies of women domestic workers come back regularly.

The editorial calls for: diplomatic pressure to get full information from Saudi authorities (arrest date, charges, evidence, legal representation, whether consular access was given); informing the families and settling return or burial of the bodies; a transparent inquiry into why the mission did not know; and a coordinated system for Bangladeshis detained or on trial abroad with quick appointment of lawyers, Bangla-language help and early diplomatic action in death-penalty cases.

key_quote_bn: সেখানে কোনো নাগরিক অভিযুক্ত হলে তাঁর সঙ্গে কনস্যুলার যোগাযোগ, আইনজীবী ও দোভাষীর ব্যবস্থা, বিচারপ্রক্রিয়া ঠিকভাবে চলছে কি না, তা নজরে রাখা মিশনের কাজের আওতার মধ্যেই পড়ে।

headline_en: The real cause must be known to prevent untimely deaths
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial on rising deaths of migrant workers: on average more than 14 bodies a day arrive, 4,060 came in January to 30 September 2026, and most deaths are recorded as 'natural' on papers that Bangladesh does not verify. It links Middle East deaths to extreme heat in construction work and says families often lose compensation and insurance.

facts.statement: Wage Earners' Welfare Board data analysed by Prothom Alo show 18,166 bodies of migrant workers arrived in Bangladesh from 2018 to 2023, an average of about 3,600 a year.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board data, as reported by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: 4,060 bodies of migrant workers arrived in Bangladesh in the nine months from January to 30 September 2026; on average more than 14 bodies a day arrive from various countries.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board data, as reported by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare data say the papers accompanying bodies give 'natural death' as the cause in 66-70% of cases and accidents and other causes in 30-34%; the cause stated by the country of death is in most cases not verified by Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment data, cited in editorial

facts.statement: Most bodies come from Saudi Arabia. Most Bangladeshi workers in the Middle East work in infrastructure construction in extreme daytime heat; migration researchers believe excess heat is the cause of the high number of deaths, and workers aged 20-30 are also dying.

Wage Earners' Welfare Board data show many workers die in road accidents on the way to and from work, workplace accidents and fires; workplace torture, murder, sexual abuse and suicide also occur, with women workers' safety a particular concern.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board data, cited in editorial

facts.statement: The editorial says families are often deprived of compensation and insurance benefits when the cause of death is recorded perfunctorily as 'natural', and that there should be no delay in bringing home bodies, including those of irregular workers.
BBS data: 23-24 lakh young people join the labour market each year, of whom 12-13 lakh find work in the country; the rest have to go abroad for a living.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics, cited in editorial

headline_en: Government recruitment of male workers for Brunei, 148 posts
summary_en: The state agency BOESL (Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited) is recruiting 148 male workers for Unity Land Sdn Bhd in Brunei across nine construction-related trades, with no educational requirement. The notice gives wages in Brunei dollars, age and experience requirements, the BDT 100 application fee, BOESL charges of BDT 56,350 (skilled) or BDT 44,850 (semi/unskilled), and a deadline of 5 October 2026, 4 pm.

facts.statement: BOESL (Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited) is recruiting 148 male workers for Brunei on a government basis for the company Unity Land Sdn Bhd; no educational qualification is required and applications close on 5 October 2026 at 4 pm.
Posts in the BOESL Brunei (Unity Land Sdn Bhd) recruitment: carpenter 20, construction worker 70, mason 20, electrician 5, truck driver 2, heavy vehicle driver 2, operator 4, plumber 10, welder 15.

Pay in the BOESL Brunei recruitment is stated in Brunei dollars without a pay period: 20 dollars (BDT 2,458.85) for carpenter, construction worker and mason; 22 dollars (BDT 2,704.72) for electrician, truck driver, heavy vehicle driver, operator, plumber and welder. The company bears accommodation cost and the employer bears air fare.
Terms for the Brunei jobs through BOESL: two-year labour contract, renewable; 8 hours of duty a day.
Applicants for the BOESL Brunei jobs must be aged 25 to 45 with at least 2 years of practical experience in the relevant trade.
Applications for the BOESL Brunei jobs must be made through the website brms.boesl.gov.bd; the application fee is BDT 100.

Candidates finally selected by the employer who pass the medical test must deposit BOESL's service charge, registration fee and incidental costs: BDT 56,350 for skilled workers and BDT 44,850 for semi-skilled/unskilled workers. The worker also bears the embassy-set visa fee and the medical test fee in Bangladesh.

BOESL warns that any person or organisation demanding money beyond the fixed service charge is to be regarded as a fraudster, that BOESL takes no cash, and that applicants should avoid cash transactions and pay no money to anyone.

headline_en: Call for technology-based coordinated effort to prevent human trafficking in Teknaf
summary_en: BRAC's Migration Programme, with Australian government funding, held workshops in Teknaf on 26 July 2026 for 42 local journalists and for law-enforcement members on trafficking and migrant smuggling by sea. Speakers called for arresting ringleaders and technology-based coordination; a reporter noted that a trawler with more than 280 people that left via the Teknaf coast sank in the Andaman Sea, and the Teknaf police chief called the area a trafficking 'red zone'.

facts.statement: A trawler loaded with more than 280 people that left through the Teknaf coast sank in the Andaman Sea; foreign organisations reported the sinking first and Teknaf journalists did not know people were being loaded on the trawler.
facts.source_in_article: Abdul Kuddus, Prothom Alo staff correspondent, speaking at the workshop

facts.statement: Teknaf Model Thana officer-in-charge Md. Saiful Islam described Teknaf as a 'red zone' for human trafficking and migrant smuggling; the workshop discussed the risky sea routes through the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea.

BRAC's Migration Programme, funded by the Australian government, held separate workshops at Central Resort, Teknaf, for 42 journalists from Teknaf and Ukhia and for members of police, RAB, BGB, APBn, Ansar and VDP on preventing human trafficking and migrant smuggling by sea.

Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police Momena Akter said trafficking does not bring remittances: remittance falls, the money stays abroad, strengthens trafficking gangs and is used to buy harmful goods such as drugs that come back into Bangladesh; she said the ringleaders must be caught.

headline_en: Broker arrested for allegedly selling a young man in Kenya after promising to send him to Italy: RAB
summary_en: RAB-10 arrested Tota Mal (62) of Shibchar, Madaripur, in Dhaka on 23 July 2026. He is accused of taking BDT 16 lakh from the family of Md. Tamim on a promise of legal travel to Italy, after which Tamim was taken to Sri Lanka, smuggled to India and then to Kenya and sold to a mafia gang; the family paid BDT 3 lakh of a BDT 5 lakh ransom demand but he has not returned.

facts.statement: A broker ring including Tota Mal took BDT 16 lakh on 28 November 2024 from the family of Md. Tamim of Uttarail area, Shibchar upazila, Madaripur, promising to send him to Italy legally, with a promise to send him that same day.
Instead of Italy, Md. Tamim was first taken to Sri Lanka, held there for some days, smuggled illegally into India, and then taken from India to Kenya and sold to a mafia gang, according to RAB.
After Tamim was taken to Kenya, a further BDT 5 lakh was demanded from his family as the condition for freeing him; the family paid BDT 3 lakh under duress but Tamim could not return to Bangladesh.

Tamim's mother filed a case under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act at Shibchar police station, Madaripur, on 15 March (the article is dated July 2026); RAB-10 began surveillance after a request from the investigating officer.

RAB-10 arrested Tota Mal (62), a resident of Bajeharchar area, Shibchar upazila, Madaripur, and an FIR-named accused in the case, in the Mirhajirbag area of Dhaka on the evening of Thursday 23 July 2026, and handed him to Shibchar police station.

headline_en: 62% of remittance comes from just five countries, Saudi Arabia on top
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show remittances of USD 3,277 crore in the first 11 months (July-May) of FY2025-26, of which USD 2,025 crore or about 62% came from Saudi Arabia, the UK, the UAE, Malaysia and the US. Saudi Arabia led for ten months but the UK overtook it in May. Analysts warn about dependence on five countries.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent a total of USD 3,277 crore in remittances to Bangladesh in the first 11 months (July-May) of FY2025-26; the top five source countries (Saudi Arabia, UK, UAE, Malaysia, US) accounted for USD 2,025 crore, about 62%.

Remittances by source in the first 11 months of FY2025-26: Saudi Arabia USD 527 crore 97 lakh (16% of the total), United Kingdom USD 468 crore 58 lakh, UAE USD 427 crore 82 lakh, Malaysia USD 322 crore, United States USD 278 crore 96 lakh.
Oman, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Singapore and Italy together sent about USD 889 crore in the 11 months, 27% of total remittances; in all about 90% of remittances came from 11 countries.

In May 2026 expatriates sent USD 344 crore 25 lakh: the UK was top with USD 65 crore 9 lakh, Saudi Arabia second with USD 54 crore 65 lakh, the UAE third with USD 46 crore 81 lakh. Remittances from the UK rose from USD 28 crore 25 lakh in July 2025, a 130% increase.

The government gives an incentive on remittances sent through the banking channel, which discourages illegal channels such as hundi, and the process of sending money through banks has been made easier than before.

Financial-sector people say remittances from the Middle East are not always stable because workers there are mostly unskilled and semi-skilled, while income from the UK and US is steadier; experts urge sending skilled workers to new markets in Europe, East Asia and the Far East.

headline_en: Bangladeshi Saifullah faces trial in the United States after extradition from Brazil
summary_en: Saifullah Al-Mamun (39), a Bangladeshi arrested in Brazil on 31 October 2019, was extradited to the United States on 8 July 2026 and appeared in federal court in Laredo, Texas, on 13 July on human-smuggling charges. He and two Bangladeshi co-accused, who have pleaded guilty and received 46 months each, allegedly moved people from Sao Paulo through Tapachula and Monterrey in Mexico and across the Rio Grande; the migrants had paid large sums to brokers in Bangladesh.

facts.statement: Saifullah Al-Mamun (39), a Bangladeshi, was extradited from Brazil to the United States on 8 July 2026 and first appeared in federal court in Laredo, Texas, on Monday 13 July 2026 to face human-smuggling charges; he had been arrested in Brazil on 31 October 2019.
facts.source_in_article: US Department of Justice press release

facts.statement: According to the US indictment, Saifullah Al-Mamun housed migrants in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and arranged their travel; Mohammad Milon Hossain kept them in Tapachula, Mexico, and sent them on to Monterrey; Moktar Hossain kept them in Monterrey and instructed them how to cross the Rio Grande river into the United States, a crossing that was hard for many to make safely.
facts.source_in_article: US court documents, via Department of Justice press release

facts.statement: The US charge sheet says the people smuggled from Bangladesh toward the United States paid large sums of money to brokers based in Bangladesh; no amount is given.

facts.statement: Co-accused Bangladeshis Mohammad Milon Hossain (46) and Moktar Hossain (38) pleaded guilty to their roles in the smuggling operation and were each sentenced to 46 months in prison.

facts.statement: Saifullah faces charges of conspiracy to bring aliens into the United States illegally, several counts of bringing aliens in for financial gain, and conspiracy to encourage and assist illegal entry; conviction on all the financial-gain counts carries 5 to a maximum of 15 years, and the conspiracy charges carry up to 10 years.

The US Justice Department's Joint Task Force Alpha (JTFA) has led to the arrest of more than 464 human smugglers and associates at home and abroad, with more than 414 convicted in the United States, and large amounts of assets forfeited.

facts.statement: Minister for Labour and Employment and for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ariful Haque Chowdhury said Malaysia's labour market reopened for Bangladesh from Monday 6 July 2026, following the prime minister's foreign visit; he said this to journalists at Sylhet Circuit House on 7 July 2026. headline_en: Woman arrested in Madaripur human-trafficking case; police looking for her son-in-law
summary_en: Police arrested Kulsum Begum (42) at Keranibat, Shibchar, Madaripur, on 13 June 2026 in a human-trafficking case in which her son-in-law Kuddus Rahman (35), named as the ringleader, is absconding. The case says the family of Sanaullah (22) paid BDT 20 lakh for direct travel to Italy; he was taken via Saudi Arabia to Libya on 29 October 2025, tortured, and a further BDT 20 lakh ransom was extracted; he has been untraceable for six months.

facts.statement: According to the FIR, Kuddus Rahman contracted to take Sanaullah (22; printed once as 'Salaullah'), son of the late Bazlu Howlader of Char Khoajpur village, Madaripur Sadar upazila, directly to Italy, and BDT 20 lakh was paid under the contract.
After the BDT 20 lakh was paid, on 29 October 2025 Sanaullah was taken via Saudi Arabia to Libya instead of directly to Italy, where the broker ring confined and tortured him.

The ring sent video messages of Sanaullah being tortured to his family and collected a further BDT 20 lakh as ransom; the family, borrowing the money, paid BDT 40 lakh in total to the trafficking ring's members.
Sanaullah has not been traced for six months; his family fears the broker ring tortured him to death.

Sanaullah's brother-in-law Roni Khan (37) filed a case in a Madaripur court on 1 June against 11 named people including Kuddus Rahman; on the court's order it was recorded as an FIR at Sadar Model Thana.

Police arrested Kulsum Begum (42), daughter of Samad Khan of Keranibat village, Shibchar upazila, on the night of Saturday 13 June 2026 at Keranibat; she was sent to jail through court on Sunday 14 June. Her son-in-law Kuddus Rahman (35), son of Ataur Rahman of Banshkandi village, Shibchar, described as the ringleader, is absconding and police operations to catch him and the other accused continue.
